6       B.   Whether  Upper  Deck  Presents  Compelling  Reasons  for  its  Proposed 
7            Redactions                                                      
8            1.   Related Documents More Than Tangentially Related to Merits  
9       As the Court previously found (ECF No. 110 at 4:6-16), Upper Deck’s proposed 
10  documents to seal are filed in connection with Parties’ summary judgment motions (ECF 
11  Nos. 74, 79).  See Pac. Marine Propellers, Inc. v. Wartsila Def., Inc., No. 17-CV-555-L-
12  NLS,
2018 WL 11457880
, at *1 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 5, 2018) (“The compelling reasons 
13  standard applies to all motions except those that are only ‘tangentially related to the merits 
14  of a case.’. . .  Defendants’ summary judgment motion is more than tangentially related to 
15  the merits”) (citing Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179).  As such, the Court finds Upper Deck’s 
16  renewed motion to seal (ECF No. 114) is subject to the “compelling reasons” standard in 
17  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179.                                               
18            2.   “Compelling Reasons” Legal Standard                        
19       Preventing the release of trade secrets generally constitutes a compelling reason to 
20  seal such documents.  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179; see also Nixon,
435 U.S. at 598
 
21  (observing that the “common-law right of inspection has bowed before the power of a court 
22  to insure that its records” are not used as “sources of business information that might harm 
23  a litigant's competitive standing”);  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co.,
727 F.3d 1214
, 1226–
24  28  (Fed.Cir.2013)  (holding  that  under  Ninth  Circuit  law,  detailed  product-specific 
25  information and internal reports are appropriate to seal under the “compelling reasons” 
26  standard where that information could be used to the company's competitive disadvantage). 
27       A  “trade  secret  may  consist  of  any  formula,  pattern,  device  or  compilation  of 
28  information  which  is  used  in  [the  party]'s  business,  and  which  gives  [the  party]  an 
1  opportunity to obtain an advantage over competitors who do not know or use it.”  In re 
2  Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x 568
, 569–70 (9th Cir. 2008) (citing Restatement of Torts § 
3  757, cmt. B); see also Clark v. Bunker,
453 F.2d 1006, 1009
 (9th Cir.1972) (adopting the 
4  Restatement  definition  and  finding  that  “a  detailed  plan  for  the  creation,  promotion, 
5  financing, and sale of contracts” constitutes a trade secret); Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., 101
6 Cal.App.4th 1443, 1455-56
,
125 Cal.Rptr.2d 277
 (2002).                    
7       Even if proposed material for sealing does not constitute a trade secret, it may still 
8  be sealable as confidential business information.  See In re Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x at 9
  569  (finding  sealable  “business  information  that  might  harm  a  litigant's  competitive 
10  standing”); see also Ctr. for Auto Safety,
809 F.3d at 1097
 (citing Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598–
11  599) (“sources of business information that might harm a litigant's competitive standing” 
12  are subject to sealing); see also In re Qualcomm Litig., No. 3:17-cv-0108-GPC-MDD, 2017
13 WL 5176922
, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 8, 2017) (sealing is warranted to prevent competitors 
14  from “gaining insight into the parties' business model and strategy”); see also Garrity 
15  Power Servs. LLC v. Samsung Elecs. Co., No. 21-MC-80159-JSC,
2021 WL 3473937
, at 
16  *1 (N.D. Cal. July 29, 2021) (“confidential business information in the form of ‘license 
17  agreements, financial terms, details of confidential licensing negotiations, and business 
18  strategies’ is sealable”).                                                
19       However, not all business information is so confidential or sensitive that it must be 
20  sealed.  See, e.g., Open Text S.A. v. Box, Inc., No. 13-04910,
2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21
  177484,
2014 WL 7368594
, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 26, 2014) (declining to seal, for example, 
22  information about a litigant's "product design and source code and highly confidential and 
23  competitively sensitive business information including usage data," in the absence of 
24  demonstrating “specific compelling reasons”); GoDaddy.com LLC v. RPost Commc'ns 
25  Ltd., No. 14-00126,
2014 WL 2117349
, at *1 (D. Ariz. May 21, 2014) ("[A] party's 
26  allegations that material is 'confidential' or 'business information' are insufficient to justify 
27  sealing court records containing such material unless the party proves the existence of 
28                                                                            
1  compelling reasons such as those set forth in Kamakana.... "[O]nly in extremely limited 
2  circumstances will confidential information actually merit the sealing of court records.").  
3       In the Ninth Circuit, trade secrets, specific pricing terms, royalty rates, and similar 
4  data are commonly sealed.  See, e.g., In re Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x 568, 569
 (9th 
5  Cir. 2008).  For information that falls outside of those categories, movants must 
6  particularly allege how their proposed redactions relate to confidential information that 
7  should be sealed.  See Perez v. Blue Mountain Farms, No. 2:13-CV-5081-RMP, 2015
8 WL 11112413
, at *4 (E.D. Wash. Sept. 28, 2015) (“Defendants' redactions and any 
9  claims of privilege or withholding of information must be explained with particularity as 
10  to why that information should be protected pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A)”); see 
11  also Ketayi v. Health Enrollment Grp., No. 3:20-CV-1198-RSH-KSC,
2023 WL 12
  12007132, at *2 (S.D. Cal. June 28, 2023)  (“Compelling reasons may exist to seal some 
13  of the redacted information in this record as confidential business information, but not for 
14  the broad redactions HII proposes.”).                                     
15       Importantly, “[t]he proponent of sealing bears the burden with respect to sealing. A 
16  failure to meet that burden means that the default posture of public access prevails.”  
17  Kamakana v. City & County of Honolulu,
447 F.3d 1172
, 1182 (9th Cir. 2006). 
18            3.   “Narrowly Tailored” Legal Standard                         
19       “Only those documents, or portions thereof, necessary to protect such sensitive 
20  information” may be sealed. Standing Order § 5.A. As such, whenever possible, the 
21  moving party must redact only what is necessary.  See Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1183; 
22  Murphy,
2012 WL 1497489
, at *2–3.  Redactions must be narrowly tailored such that only 
23  information that meets the compelling reasons standard is redacted. See Kamakana, 447 
24  F.3d at 1183 (highlighting the “limited and clear” nature and specificity of the redactions); 
25  ImprimisRx, LLC v. OSRX, Inc., No. 21-cv-01305-BAS-DL,
2023 WL 7029210
, at *4 
26  (S.D. Cal. Oct. 24, 2023) (rejecting redactions that were insufficiently tailored). The 
27  moving party must provide the compelling reason justifying the proposed redactions. Foltz, 
28
331 F.3d at 1135
.                                                         
1       Litigation predicated upon contracts cannot be conducted in secret. JBS Packerland, 
2  Inc. v. Phillips Cattle Co., Inc., No. 24-cv-01299-BAS-MSB,
2024 WL 4280960
, at *2 
3  (S.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2024).  The public has the right to know the gist of the underlying 
4  agreements in order to understand the court’s rulings.
Id.
  Accordingly, mere vague or 
5  ambiguous references to sealed documents, without any discussion of the substance of the 
6  sealed documents, do not meet the compelling reasons standard.  See Nia v. Bank of Am., 
7  N.A., No. 21-cv-1799-BAS-BGS,
2024 WL 171659
, at *9 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2024); 
8  ImprimisRx, LLC,
2023 WL 7029210
, at *5.  Information already available to the public 
9  also cannot meet the compelling reasons standard.  See
id. at 1184
.       
10            4.   Analysis of Compelling Reasons                             
11                 i.   Financial Data (e.g., Gross Revenue Amount, and Sales Data) 
12                 and Damages Calculation                                    
13       “Sales data may constitute a trade secret if it is not readily ascertainable from a public 
14  source but instead developed with a substantial amount of time, effort, and money.”  Yeiser 
15  Rsch. & Dev. LLC v. Teknor Apex Co.,
281 F. Supp. 3d 1021
, 1046 (S.D. Cal. 2017).  Here, 
16  it is apparent that Pixels has expended substantial effort to calculate its sales data and gross 
17  revenue from the various spreadsheets, tables, and expert reports Upper Deck moves to 
18  seal.  The Court has also previously found that Pixels’ financial data is subject to sealing.  
19  (ECF No. 110 at 10:21–11:20.)                                             
20       Thus, the Court GRANTS Upper Deck’s request to seal Pixels’ financial data—
21  including in sealing Exhibit F to Upper Deck’s motion to seal (ECF No. 102), which the 
22  Court has previously found to be sealable (ECF No. 110 at 11:4-6).  Along the same vein, 
23  the  Court  also  GRANTS  sealing  experts’  damages  calculations  based  upon  Pixels’ 
24  financial data.  (Id. at 10:21–11:20.)                                    
25                 ii.  Licensing Agreement Terms                             
26       The Ninth Circuit has held that licensing agreement terms are sealable trade secrets 
27  when such terms provide a plan for the formation and sale of contracts.  In re Elec. Arts, 
28  Inc., 298 F. App'x at 569–70 (finding license agreement to be a trade secret); France 
1  Telecom S.A. v. Marvell Semiconductor Inc., No. 12-CV-04967-WHO,
2014 WL 4965995
, 
2  at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 3, 2014) (“the information at issue—terms of a license agreement—
3  constitutes trade secrets and is properly sealed”).  Those terms may constitute trade secrets 
4  because their public disclosure may hinder the trade secret holder’s market competitiveness 
5  and participation.  See e.g., In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig., 
6  No. C 09-1967 CW,
2014 WL 662545
, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 20, 2014) (“Because the public 
7  disclosure of some of these terms may undermine NCAA's ability to negotiate future 
8  licensing agreements with other broadcasters, these terms may be sealed.”).  
9       However, there are limitations on the extent to which terms of a licensing agreement 
10  can be sealed.  For example, if certain terms are “otherwise publicly known,” they may not 
11  be sealable.  Huawei Techs., Co, Ltd v. Samsung Elecs. Co, Ltd.,
340 F. Supp. 3d 934
, 1004 
12  (N.D.  Cal.  2018).    Additionally,  if  terms  of  licensing  agreements  that  appear  to  be 
13  boilerplate contractual terms, courts may require the moving party to “explain[] why 
14  [those] provisions are so unique to that agreement that disclosure would cause significant 
15  harm.”
Id.
  Further, even when courts have found licensing terms to constitute trade 
16  secrets, they have still limited permissible redactions to only specific portions of those 
17  clauses.  In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig.,
2014 WL 662545
, 
18  at *1 (“only the specific dollar amounts. . . may be sealed”); O'Bannon v. Nat'l Collegiate 
19  Athletic Ass'n, No. C 09-3329 CW,
2014 WL 12997312
, at *1 (N.D. Cal. June 10, 2014) 
20  (same).                                                                   
21                      a.   Royalty   Rate,  Minimum     Guarantee,  and     
22                      Compensation Clauses                                  
23       It is well-established in the Ninth Circuit that “pricing terms, royalty rates, and 
24  guaranteed minimum payment terms” are sealable trade secrets.  In re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 
25  F. App'x at 569–70; see also Clark v. Bunker,
453 F.2d 1006, 1009
 (9th Cir.1972) (adopting 
26  the Restatement definition and finding that “a detailed plan for the creation, promotion, 
27  financing, and sale of contracts” constitutes a trade secret) (citing Whyte v. Schlage Lock 
28  Co.,
101 Cal.App.4th 1443, 1455-56
,
125 Cal.Rptr.2d 277
 (2002)).          
1       Thus, the Court GRANTS sealing the specific numerical values of royalty rate 
2  minimum guarantee and compensation terms.  See In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & 
3  Likeness Licensing Litig.,
2014 WL 662545
, at *1 (“only the specific dollar amounts. . . 
4  may be sealed”); O'Bannon,
2014 WL 12997312

5  values of royalty rates, minimum guarantee, and compensation should also be sealed in

, *2 (finding compelling 
9  reasons  to  seal  documents  containing  information  revealing  business  and  marketing 
10  strategy and product development).  Accordingly, the Court GRANTS sealing personal 
11  service-related terms.                                                    
12                      e.   Third-Party Information (e.g., Names)            
13       The identities of third parties are generally not sealable as trade secrets unless the 
14  movant “provide[s] a particularized showing that specific harm will result if the [identities 
15  are] made publicly available.”  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., No. 11-CV-01846 LHK 
16  PSG,
2012 WL 4120541
, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 18, 2012); see also Fitzhenry-Russell v. 
17  Dr. Pepper Snapple Grp., Inc., No. 17-CV-00564 NC,
2018 WL 10472795
, at *2 (N.D. 
18  Cal. Apr. 23, 2018) (“The identity of Dr. Pepper's third-party vender, Givaudan is not 
19  sealable as a trade secret under the compelling reasons standard”).  Here, Upper Deck has 
20  not provided any justification for how revealing the identities of third parties in the 
21  contracts would result in particularized harm to its market position.  Further, Upper Deck 
22  has failed to allege how third-party information involves any other privacy interests that 
23  “outweigh the traditional right of public access” in Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178.  See also 
24  Bunsow De Mory LLP v. N. Forty Consulting LLC, No. 20-CV-04997-JSC,
2021 WL 25
  4521143, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 22, 2021) (rejecting motion to seal because “the names of 
26  third-parties in this action constitute neither trade secrets nor confidential information”).  
27  Though the identities of third parties in licensing agreements may be sealable in some 
28  circumstance, such as when the “existence of the agreement[s]. . .  [are] not otherwise 
1  publicly known,” Upper Deck has failed to allege any such circumstances here.  See 
2  Huawei Techs., Co, Ltd v. Samsung Elecs. Co, Ltd.,
340 F. Supp. 3d 934, 1004
 (N.D. Cal. 
3  2018).  Thus, the Court DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s requested   
4  redactions of third-party information.                                    
5                      f.   Sublicenses, Dates, Term Lengths of Agreements   
6       Boilerplate contract terms are generally not sealable.  Virun, Inc. v. Cymbiotika, 
7  LLC, No. 822CV00325SSSDFMX,
2022 WL 17401698
, at *2 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 19, 2022).  
8  “Form contracts . . . that do not contain any confidential information may nevertheless be 
9  sealed if” their dissemination would create a competitive disadvantage.
Id.
  The excerpts 
10  Upper Deck seeks to seal regarding sublicensing, agreement dates, and agreement term 
11  lengths  are  common  provisions  in  licensing  agreements.    Cf  Novartis  Vaccines  & 
12  Diagnostics, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc., No. 5:21-CV-04874-EJD,
2022 WL 689005
, at *2 
13  (N.D. Cal. Feb. 14, 2022) (“parties provide no support for why a general description of the 
14  nature  of  the  Licensing  Agreement—particularly  a  general  description  that  reveals 
15  provisions and terms common to virtually all patent licensing agreements—should be 
16  sealed.”)  While it may be true that competitors could gain a commercial advantage upon 
17  discovering the term length of the agreements at issue in this litigation, Upper Deck has 
18  not made a particularized showing of why that may be beyond merely noting that the 
19  aforementioned terms constitute trade secrets.  See In re Sotera Wireless, Inc.,
591 B.R. 20 453, 462
 (S.D. Cal. 2018), aff'd,
794 F. App'x 625
 (9th Cir. 2020) (“[T]he mere statement 
21  that something is a trade secret falls far short of what the Court needs to find that [movant] 
22  has met its burden of proof. . .”).  Additionally, Upper Deck does not provide additional 
23  reasoning for why such terms should be sealed—meaning Upper Deck has failed to 
24  overcome the presumption of public access.  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178.  Thus, the Court 
25  DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s requests to redact provisions regarding 
26  sublicensing, agreement dates, and agreement term lengths.                
27                      g.   Damages-Related  Licensing  Terms  (e.g.,  Related  to 
28                      Violation)                                            
1       Upper Deck has failed to provide particularized justification for why licensing 
2  provisions relating to damages constitute either trade secrets or confidential information.  
3  See In re Sotera Wireless, Inc.,
591 B.R. at 462
 (“[T]he mere statement that something is 
4  a trade secret falls far short of what the Court needs to find that [movant] has met its burden 
5  of proof. . .”); cf GoDaddy.com LLC v. RPost Commc'ns Ltd., No. CV-14-00126-PHX-
6  JAT,
2016 WL 1158851
, at *5 (D. Ariz. Mar. 24, 2016) (“Whether Mr. Smith properly 
7  apportioned damages is an issue that GoDaddy strongly disputes. . . and thus, the public 
8  has a high interest in this information to understand the judicial process. In the absence of 
9  compelling reasons as to why this information merits sealing, the Court will not authorize 
10  Exhibit 4 to be sealed.”).                                                
11       Thus, the Court finds Upper Deck has failed to meet its burden of proof to overcome 
12  the  “traditional  right  of  public  access,”  Kamakana,  447  F.3d  at  1178,  and  DENIES 
13  WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s request to seal damages provisions of licensing 
14  agreements.                                                               
15                 iii.  Lease Agreement Terms                                
16       Upper Deck moves to seal portions of ECF Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 10 regarding commercial 
17  lease agreements, including the text detailing the amount of security deposit, length of term 
18  of the agreement, and the amount of rent.  Courts within the Ninth Circuit have held that, 
19  without further explaining why terms of a lease should be subject to sealing, movants 
20  cannot “outweigh the traditional right of public access” by merely stating that such terms 
21  are  confidential.    MTO  Summerlin  LLC  v.  Shops  at  Summerlin  N.,  LP,  No. 
22  218CV00737GMNPAL,
2019 WL 1261105
, at *4 (D. Nev. Mar. 19, 2019) (applying 
23  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178).  Similarly, here, Upper Deck does not explain how lease 
24  terms in the record constitute either trade secrets or otherwise confidential information that 
25  should be sealed beyond merely stating they should be sealed due to “privacy” concerns.  
26  Thus, the Court DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s proposed redactions 
27  to seal lease terms.                                                      
28                 iv.  Jordan Signature                                      
1       Upper Deck also moves to redact Jordan’s signature from ECF Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 7.  
2  However,  Upper  Deck  has  failed  to  allege  that  Jordan’s  signature  is  “not  readily 
3  ascertainable from a public source” such that it is a trade secret, or that such data should 
4  be protected on any other ground of confidentiality.  See Yeiser Rsch. & Dev. LLC ,
281 F. 5
  Supp. 3d at 1046.  In absence of any particularized showing, the Court finds that Upper 
6  Deck has not met its burden of proof to overcome the presumption of public access. 
7  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179.                                               
8                 v.   Exhibit 105                                           
9       “An unsupported assertion of ‘unfair advantage’ to competitors without explaining 
10  ‘how  a  competitor  would  use  th[e]  information  to  obtain  an  unfair  advantage’  is 
11  insufficient.” Hodges v. Apple, Inc., No. 13–cv–01128–WHO,
2013 WL 6070408
, at *2 
12  (N.D. Cal. Nov. 18, 2013).  Since Upper Deck has not provided reasoning for how the 
13  email chain discussion would be “advantageous for competitors and unscrupulous actors 
14  to  know”  beyond  stating  as  such  (ECF  No.  114  at  9:3-7),  the  Court  also  DENIES 
15  WITHOUT PREJUDICE sealing Exhibit 105 to Pixels’ motion to seal (ECF No. 78)—
16  which concerns how Upper Deck may use Jordan’s image to develop new products.

18       Before  the  Court  is  Defendant  Pixels.com’s  (“Pixels”)  motion  to  exclude  the 
19  testimony  of  Plaintiff  The  Upper  Deck  Company’s  (“Upper  Deck”)  expert  witness, 
20  Christian Tregillis.  (ECF No. 77.)  Upper Deck opposes.  (ECF No. 100.)  Pixels replies.  
21  (ECF No. 108.)  The Court finds this motion suitable for determination on the papers 
22  submitted and without oral argument.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 78(b); CivLR 7.1(d).  For the 
23  following reasons, the Court DENIES Pixels’ motion (ECF No. 77).          
24  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
25       On March 26, 2024, Upper Deck commenced this action against Pixels.  (Compl., 
26  Ex. 1 to Notice of Removal, ECF No. 1.)  On May 28, 2024, Pixels removed the action to 
27  federal court.  (Notice of Removal.)  Upper Deck subsequently filed a First Amended 
28  Complaint (“FAC”) alleging violation and deprivation of the right of publicity, violations 
1  of the Lanham Act, registered trademark infringement, violation of California’s Unfair 
2  Competition Law, and California common law unfair competition.  (FAC ¶ 1, ECF No. 
3  24.)                                                                      
4       At the center of this dispute, Upper Deck claims that Pixels has marketed and sold 
5  wall décor featuring images that infringe upon Upper Deck’s trademarks and Michael 
6  Jordan’s name, image, likeness, and publicity rights.  (Id. ¶ 25.)  Upper Deck brings this 
7  action pursuant to an exclusive agreement with Jordan (the “Jordan Agreement”) for the 
8  use of his name, image, likeness, and other publicity rights.  (Id. ¶ 19.)  Upper Deck asserts 
9  the agreement also gives Upper Deck the right to commence actions on behalf of Jordan 
10  for infringement of the rights assigned in the Jordan Agreement.  (Id. ¶ 20.)  
11       In support of its claims, Upper Deck has designated Christian Tregillis as a damages 
12  expert to opine on the fair market value of Pixels’ alleged unauthorized use of Jordan’s 
13  rights.  (Expert Report of Christian Tregillis (“Tregillis Report”) ¶ 1, ECF No. 82-4.)  Pixels 
14  moves to exclude Tregillis’s testimony, contending that his methodology is unreliable and 
15  based upon insufficient facts and data.  (ECF No. 77 at 2:7-10.)  Pixels also contends that 
16  the premium multiplier Tregillis uses in his fair market value calculation is unreliable and 
17  that Tregillis’s two “Evidence Indicates” opinions are irrelevant.  (Id. at 13:5-8, 21:8-12.) 
18  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
19       Federal Rule of Evidence 702 establishes several requirements for admissibility of 
20  expert opinion evidence: (1) the witness must be sufficiently qualified as an expert by 
21  knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education; (2) the scientific, technical, or other 
22  specialized knowledge must “help the trier of fact” either “to understand the evidence” or 
23  “to determine a fact in issue”; (3) the testimony must be “based on sufficient facts or data”; 
24  (4) the testimony must be “the product of reliable principles and methods”; and (5) the 
25  expert must reliably apply the principles and methods to the facts of the case. 
26       Under Daubert and its progeny, the trial court is tasked with assuring that expert 
27  testimony “both rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task at hand.”  Daubert 
28  v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 597 (1993).  “Expert opinion testimony is 
1  relevant if the knowledge underlying it has a valid connection to the pertinent inquiry.  And 
2  it is reliable if the knowledge underlying it has a reliable basis in the knowledge and 
3  experience of the relevant discipline.”  Primiano v. Cook, 598 F.3d 558, 565 (9th Cir. 2010) 
4  (citation modified).  Shaky but admissible evidence is to be attacked by cross-examination, 
5  contrary evidence, and careful instruction on the burden of proof, not exclusion.  Daubert, 
6  509 U.S. at 596.  The judge is “to screen the jury from unreliable nonsense opinions, but 
7  not exclude opinions merely because they are impeachable.”  Alaska Rent-A-Car, Inc. v. 
8  Avis Budget Grp., Inc., 738 F.3d 960, 969 (9th Cir. 2013).  In its role as gatekeeper, the 
9  trial court “is not tasked with deciding whether the expert is right or wrong, just whether 
10  his [or her] testimony has substance such that it would be helpful to a jury.”  Id. at 969–70. 
11       The tests for admissibility in general, and reliability in particular, are flexible.  
12  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 564.  The Supreme Court has provided several factors to determine 
13  reliability: (1) whether a theory or technique is testable; (2) whether it has been published 
14  in peer-reviewed literature; (3) the error rate of the theory or technique; and (4) whether it 
15  has been generally accepted in the relevant scientific community.  Elsayed Mukhtar v. Cal. 
16  State Univ., Hayward, 299 F.3d 1053, 1064 (9th Cir. 2002) (summarizing Daubert, 509 
17  U.S. at 592–94), overruled on other grounds by Est. of Barabin v. AstenJohnson, Inc., 740 
18  F.3d 457, 460 (9th Cir. 2014).  These factors are meant to be “helpful, not definitive.”  
19  Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael, 526 U.S. 137, 151 (1999).  The court “has discretion to 
20  decide how to test an expert’s reliability as well as whether the testimony is reliable, based 
21  on the particular circumstances of the particular case.”  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 564 (citation 
22  modified).  “[T]he test under Daubert is not the correctness of the expert’s conclusions but 
23  the soundness of his [or her] methodology.”  Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc., 43 F.3d 
24  1311, 1318 (9th Cir. 1995).  Once the threshold established by Rule 702 is met, the expert 
25  may testify, and the fact finder decides how much weight to give that testimony.  Primiano, 
26  598 F.3d at 565.                                                          
27       After admissibility is established to the court’s satisfaction, attacks aimed at the 
28  weight of the evidence are the province of the fact finder, not the judge.  Pyramid Techs., 
1  Inc. v. Hartford Cas. Ins. Co., 752 F.3d 807, 814 (9th Cir. 2014).  The court should not 
2  make credibility determinations that are reserved for the jury.  Id.      
3  III.  ANALYSIS                                                            
4       Pixels argues Tregillis’s opinions are inadmissible because Tregillis (1) employs a 
5  faulty and unreliable methodology; (2) relies upon insufficient facts and data; and (3) 
6  provides irrelevant factual opinions.  (ECF No. 77 at 2:7-17.)            
7       Pixels does not challenge Tregillis’s qualifications.  (See generally Mot.)  Tregillis 
8  holds an M.B.A. in Finance and Accounting.  (Tregillis Report at App. A.)  He has more 
9  than thirty years of experience analyzing financial, accounting, economic, statistical, and 
10  market issues, primarily relating to disputes, valuations, and license agreements covering 
11  intellectual property rights.  (Id.)  Tregillis has held leadership positions with many public 
12  accounting and licensing professional groups.  (Id.)  He is also accredited in Business 
13  Valuation and certified in Financial Forensics, Public Accounting, and Licensing.  (Id.)  
14  Thus, finding Tregillis sufficiently qualified to render his opinion, the Court turns to Pixels’ 
15  arguments for exclusion.                                                  
16       A.   Methodology                                                     
17       Tregillis  calculates  the  fair  market  value  of  Pixels’  use  of  Jordan’s  rights  by 
18  analyzing comparable licenses for rights similar to those used by Pixels as a starting point 
19  to construct a hypothetical license.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 118-21.)  Tregillis then adjusts the 
20  value of the benchmark comparable license to account for the other athletes included in the 
21  benchmark license, the length of time of Pixels’ use, and the fact that Pixels’ use of Jordan’s 
22  rights was not subject to any quality assurance or approval clauses.  (Id. ¶¶ 122, 126.)  
23  Pixels  argues  that  the  benchmark  agreement  chosen  by  Tregillis  is  insufficiently 
24  comparable and that Tregillis makes improper assumptions to inflate the value of the 
25  benchmark license.  (ECF No. 77 at 9:19–10:1.)                            
26       Damages determined through a hypothetical license are appropriate “provided the 
27  amount is not based on undue speculation.”  See Polar Bear Prods., Inc. v. Timex Corp., 
28  384 F.3d 700, 709 (9th Cir. 2004) (citation modified); see also Marketquest Grp., Inc. v. 
1  BIC Corp., 316 F. Supp. 3d 1234, 1300 (S.D. Cal. 2018) (permitting hypothetical licensing 
2  damages in a Lanham Act dispute “if the evidence provides a sufficiently reliable basis to 
3  calculate such damages”).  “The touchstone for hypothetical-license damages is ‘the range 
4  of [the license’s] reasonable market value.’”  Oracle Corp. v. SAP AG, 765 F.3d 1081, 
5  1088 (9th Cir. 2014) (quoting Polar Bear Prods., 384 F.3d at 709).  “The question, 
6  therefore, is not what the owner would have charged, but rather what is the fair market 
7  value.”  Id. (citation modified).                                         
8       Accordingly,  as  a  starting  point,  Tregillis’s  methodology  of  constructing  a 
9  hypothetical license to determine the fair market value of Pixels’ use of Jordan’s rights is 
10  an accepted and reliable method to calculate damages in an intellectual property dispute.  
11  See Polar Bear Prods., 384 F.3d at 709.  The Court now considers the reliability of the 
12  facts underlying Tregillis’s methodology and opinions.                    
13            1.   Underlying Facts and Data                                  
14       Tregillis determines the Trends Agreement to be the most comparable to the facts at 
15  issue here and uses this agreement as the benchmark for his hypothetical license analysis.  
16  (Tregillis Report ¶ 121.)  The Trends Agreement was a licensing agreement between 
17  Brevettar,  described  as  “the  exclusive  licensing  agent  for  Upper  Deck,”  and  Trends 
18  International, LLC.  (Id. ¶ 50.)  The Trends Agreement granted Trends a license to 
19  manufacture, distribute, and sell collector’s edition posters and calendars featuring the 
20  name, image, likeness, signature, and statistical data of Michael Jordan, Wayne Gretzky, 
21  and Tiger Woods.  (Id.)  A later amendment to the Trends Agreement also allowed Trends 
22  to sell canvas wall décor.  (Id. ¶¶ 56–57.)                               
23       Pixels argues that the Trends Agreement is an improper comparable because Upper 
24  Deck  was not  a  party to it,  Upper Deck  did not  receive  royalty  payments  from  the 
25  agreement, and the Trends Agreement was not effective until two and a half years after 
26  Pixels alleged unauthorized sales began.  (ECF No. 77 at 10:4–11:1.)  Pixels also asserts 
27  that Tregillis improperly inflated the annual minimum guarantee and sales made under the 
28  Trends Agreement by relying on a later amendment to the Trends Agreement that increased 
1  the annual minimum guarantee and added another category of products covered by the 
2  Trends  Agreement.    (Id.  at  11:2–12:10.)    Finally,  Pixels  claims  Tregillis  improperly 
3  deflated the annual minimum guarantee payment to account for the other athletes included 
4  in the Trends Agreement.  (Id. at 12:11-20.)                              
5       When  constructing  a  hypothetical  license,  “the  licenses  relied  on  by  the 
6  [rightsholder] in proving damages [must be] sufficiently comparable to the hypothetical 
7  license at issue in suit.”  Lucent Techs., Inc. v. Gateway, Inc., 580 F.3d 1301, 1325 (Fed. 
8  Cir. 2009); see also Marketquest Grp., 316 F. Supp. 3d at 1300 (requiring a “sufficiently 
9  reliable basis to calculate. . . damages” in absence of a prior licensing agreement).  As such, 
10  “alleging a loose or vague comparability between different technologies or licenses does 
11  not suffice.”  LaserDynamics, Inc. v. Quanta Comput., Inc., 694 F.3d 51, 79 (Fed. Cir. 
12  2012).  However, any hypothetical license analysis “necessarily involves an element of 
13  approximation and uncertainty.”  Lucent, 580 F.3d at 1325 (citation modified); see also 
14  Skydive Ariz., Inc. v. Quattrocchi, 673 F.3d 1105, 1113 (9th Cir. 2012) (“We emphasize 
15  that section 1117 confers a wide scope of discretion upon the district judge in fashioning a 
16  remedy.”  (citation modified)).  “[T]he fact that a license is not perfectly analogous 
17  generally goes to the weight of the evidence, not its admissibility.”  Ericsson, Inc. v. D-
18  Link Sys., Inc., 773 F.3d 1201, 1227 (Fed. Cir. 2014); see also Roblox Corp. v. WowWee 
19  Grp. Ltd., No. 22-cv-04476-SI, 2024 WL 4057418, at *14 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 3, 2024) 
20  (rejecting objections that the benchmark license was not sufficiently comparable as the 
21  objections went to the weight, not admissibility of the expert’s analysis). 
22       Here, the Trends Agreement concerned the same rights at issue in this case, Jordan’s 
23  name, image, likeness, and publicity rights.  (Tregillis Report ¶ 50.)  Further, the Trends 
24  Agreement covered the same types of products as those at issue here—posters, calendars, 
25  and wall décor.  (Id. ¶ 121.)  The Trends Agreement also covered products similarly priced 
26  to those sold by Pixels.  (Id.)  Consequently, the Court finds the Trends Agreement 
27  sufficiently comparable to serve as a reliable basis for the hypothetical license analysis 
28  Tregillis conducts.                                                       
1       Each  of  Pixels’  arguments  about  the  specific  terms  of  the  Trends  Agreement, 
2  including the parties to it, the time period it covered, the products it included, the annual 
3  minimum  guarantee,  and  the  proportion  of  sales  attributed to  each  athlete  under  the 
4  Agreement, bears on the Agreement’s comparability with the conduct at issue here.  As 
5  such, these arguments go to the weight of the evidence, not its admissibility.1  See Ericsson, 
6  773 F.3d at 1227; Roblox Corp., 2024 WL 4057418, at *14.                  
7            2.   The Premium Multiplier                                     
8       After identifying the Trends Agreement as the best benchmark for his hypothetical 
9  license analysis, Tregillis uses a premium multiplier to adjust for the fact that Pixels’ use 
10  of Jordan’s rights was not authorized and not subject to the quality assurance and approval 
11  clauses typically included in Jordan’s licensing agreements.  (Tregillis Report ¶ 122.)  
12  Tregillis calculates this multiplier by comparing two similar situations where Jordan’s 
13  rights were used, one of which was authorized (the “Hanes Transaction”) and one of which 
14  was unauthorized (the “Panini Settlement”).  (Id. ¶¶ 124-25.)  Tregillis compares the values 
15  of those transactions to calculate the percentage premium for unauthorized uses of Jordan’s 
16  rights.  (Id.)  Pixels argues that the application of this premium multiplier is unreliable and 
17  that the Hanes Transaction and Panini Settlement are not reliably comparable to the 
18  conduct at issue here.  (ECF No. 77 at 13:5-12.)                          
19        Hypothetical  license  analysis  requires  experts  to  make  adjustments  to  the 
20  benchmark  agreement  to  best  fit  the  facts  at  issue.    Indeed,  upward  and  downward 
21  adjustments to a benchmark agreement are commonly and reliably used in hypothetical 
22  license analyses.  See, e.g., Oracle Am., Inc. v. Google Inc., 847 F. Supp. 2d 1178, 1184 
23  (N.D. Cal. 2012) (finding an upward adjustment based on several factually supported 
24  factors to be proper under Daubert); Juno Therapeutics, Inc. v. Kite Pharma, Inc., No. 
25                                                                            
26

7       Here, the adjustment Tregillis applies is neither created out of whole cloth nor based 
8  on mere speculation, as Pixels asserts.  Rather, Tregillis demonstrates the necessity of this 
9  premium  adjustment  by  discussing  Jordan’s  carefully  tailored  brand  and  restrictive

14  the premium multiplier calculation and its application to the hypothetical license are

16       The cases cited by Tregillis in support of the premium multiplier—and also relied 
17  on by both Pixels and Upper Deck in their briefings—tend to support the reliability of the 
18  premium multiplier in this case.  For example, the Garrapata court, in the default judgment 
19  context, ultimately recognized that “a $2 million figure appropriately compensates [the 
20  plaintiff] for the premium that would be necessarily required to induce it to agree to such

23  premium may be appropriate to incorporate into the damages award to account for the fact

25  a reasonable representation of the fair market value of Mr. Eastwood’s services in lending 
26  his influential and known name to a hidden metatag campaign for products he likely would 
27  have been unwilling to endorse in the first place.”).  Although Pixels is correct that the 
28  Garrapata court rejected the extent of the premium proposed by the plaintiff, the court 
1  ultimately endorsed the principle of applying a premium to account for unauthorized use.  
2  Id. at *6–7.  Tregillis applies that same principle here.                 
3       Likewise, the Edmondson court did not condemn the use of any premium multipliers, 
4  but it rejected the premium multiplier applied by the expert because it was speculative.

6  at *6 (M.D. Fla. Aug. 31, 2017).  The Edmondson expert’s treble multiplier appeared to be 
7  “a formula entirely of [the expert’s] imagination.”  Id.  But here, in contrast, Tregillis backs 
8  up his premium multiplier by demonstrating why it is appropriate in this case and by 
9  calculating  the  premium  multiplier  through  an  evidence-based  comparative  analysis.  
10  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 88–106, 124-25.)                                     
11       Pixels further attacks on the premium multiplier are similarly unpersuasive.2  Pixels 
12  argues that Tregillis does not properly verify or discuss the Hanes Transaction and Panini 
13  Settlement before using them in his analysis.  (ECF No. 77 at 14:16-20, 15:14–16:8.)  This 
14  argument is unconvincing, as Tregillis spends paragraphs of his report, supported by 
15  citations to the record, discussing the Hanes Transaction and Panini Settlement as well as 
16  how he uses them in his analysis.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 85–86, 124-25.)   
17       Pixels’  next  argument  that  the  Hanes  Transaction  and  Panini  Settlement  are 
18  insufficiently comparable to Pixels’ conduct here misses the point of how Tregillis uses 
19  these two situations.  (ECF No. 77 at 16:28–17:1.)  Tregillis does not use the Hanes 
20  Transaction  and  Panini  Settlement  as  comparable  to  this  case  for  the  purpose  of 
21  hypothetical license analysis; rather, he uses them in a comparative analysis to determine 
22  the value of Jordan’s rights when their use is not subject to any quality assurance or 
23  approval clauses.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 124-25.)

11       B.   The “Evidence Indicates” Opinions                               
12       In addition to his opinions on the economic harm to Upper Deck and Jordan and the 
13  revenues earned by Pixels, Tregillis offers two “Evidence Indicates” opinions.  First, 
14  “Evidence indicates that, as Upper Deck values its relationship with Jordan, one of the 
15  world’s most iconic athletes and personalities, Upper Deck protects both its rights and 
16  Jordan’s rights, while also ensuring it only produces and/or approves high-quality products 
17  that feature appropriate and value-enhancing uses of Jordan’s rights of publicity and 
18  trademarks.”  (Tregillis Report § 1.1.)  And second, “Evidence indicates that the use made 
19  by Pixels is unauthorized and would not have been authorized by Jordan and/or Upper 
20  Deck.”  (Id.)  Pixels argues these opinions are irrelevant and should be excluded.  (ECF 
21  No. 77 at 21:8-12.)                                                       
22       Expert testimony is relevant if it is sufficiently tied to the facts of the case such that 
23  it will “assist the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue.”  
24  See Daubert, 509 U.S. at 591 (citation modified).  The Ninth Circuit has found expert 
25  testimony is relevant if it “logically advances a material aspect of the proposing party’s 
26  case.”  Daubert, 43 F.3d at 1315; see also Primiano, 598 F.3d at 565 (“Expert opinion 
27  testimony is relevant if the knowledge underlying it has a valid connection to the pertinent 
28  inquiry.”  (citation modified)).                                          
1       Pixels primarily argues that the “Evidence Indicates” opinions are irrelevant because 
2  they assert facts favorable to Upper Deck that are not relevant to assisting the jury, and as 
3  such, they should be excluded under Federal Rules of Evidence 702 and 403.  (ECF No. 
4  77 at 21:8-12.)  However, the Court finds that the two “Evidence Indicates” opinions will 
5  aid the jury in understanding Tregillis’s hypothetical license analysis.  The “Evidence 
6  Indicates” opinions shed light on the fair market value of Jordan’s rights as Pixels used 
7  them and demonstrate the necessity of the premium multiplier.  More specifically, the

9  and typically license them.  Hence, the Court finds that these opinions are relevant for the 
10  jury’s consideration and fall within the scope of Tregillis’s expert testimony.  See Daubert, 
11  43 F.3d at 1315; Primiano, 598 F.3d at 565.                               
12       Pixels also seems to raise an objection to the “Evidence Indicates” opinions under

16  is not testifying about ‘authorization’ in a liability sense (he assumes this as all damages 
17  experts do . . .), but rather that the use Pixels made would not have been contractually 
18  approved or authorized by Jordan because of the images used and types of products sold.  
19  This goes to brand standards, not liability.”  (ECF No. 100 at 22:20-24.) 
20       Under Federal Rule of Evidence 704, “[a]n opinion is not objectionable just because 
21  it embraces an ultimate issue.”  Rather, the basic approach to opinions is to admit them 
22  when helpful to the trier of fact.  Fed. R. Evid. 704 advisory committee’s notes.  Experts 
23  may not, however, offer opinions embodying legal conclusions.  See id. (clarifying Rule 
24  704 as not permitting “the admission of opinions which would merely tell the jury what 
25  result to reach”).                                                        
26       Here, the Court agrees that Tregillis’s second “Evidence Indicates” opinion goes to 
27  brand standards and addresses how the fair market value of Jordan’s rights is impacted 
28  when subject to quality assurance and approval clauses.  This opinion lays the foundation

3  24.)                                                                      
4       At the center of this dispute, Upper Deck claims that Pixels has marketed and sold 
5  wall décor featuring images that infringe upon Upper Deck’s trademarks and Michael 
6  Jordan’s name, image, likeness, and publicity rights.  (Id. ¶ 25.)  Upper Deck brings this 
7  action pursuant to an exclusive agreement with Jordan (the “Jordan Agreement”) for the 
8  use of his name, image, likeness, and other publicity rights.  (Id. ¶ 19.)  Upper Deck asserts 
9  the agreement also gives Upper Deck the right to commence actions on behalf of Jordan 
10  for infringement of the rights assigned in the Jordan Agreement.  (Id. ¶ 20.)  
11       In support of its claims, Upper Deck has designated Christian Tregillis as a damages 
12  expert to opine on the fair market value of Pixels’ alleged unauthorized use of Jordan’s 
13  rights.  (Expert Report of Christian Tregillis (“Tregillis Report”) ¶ 1, ECF No. 82-4.)  Pixels 
14  moves to exclude Tregillis’s testimony, contending that his methodology is unreliable and 
15  based upon insufficient facts and data.  (ECF No. 77 at 2:7-10.)  Pixels also contends that 
16  the premium multiplier Tregillis uses in his fair market value calculation is unreliable and 
17  that Tregillis’s two “Evidence Indicates” opinions are irrelevant.  (Id. at 13:5-8, 21:8-12.) 
18  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
19       Federal Rule of Evidence 702 establishes several requirements for admissibility of 
20  expert opinion evidence: (1) the witness must be sufficiently qualified as an expert by 
21  knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education; (2) the scientific, technical, or other 
22  specialized knowledge must “help the trier of fact” either “to understand the evidence” or 
23  “to determine a fact in issue”; (3) the testimony must be “based on sufficient facts or data”; 
24  (4) the testimony must be “the product of reliable principles and methods”; and (5) the 
25  expert must reliably apply the principles and methods to the facts of the case. 
26       Under Daubert and its progeny, the trial court is tasked with assuring that expert 
27  testimony “both rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task at hand.”  Daubert 
28  v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc.,
509 U.S. 579, 597
 (1993).  “Expert opinion testimony is 
1  relevant if the knowledge underlying it has a valid connection to the pertinent inquiry.  And 
2  it is reliable if the knowledge underlying it has a reliable basis in the knowledge and 
3  experience of the relevant discipline.”  Primiano v. Cook,
598 F.3d 558
, 565 (9th Cir. 2010) 
4  (citation modified).  Shaky but admissible evidence is to be attacked by cross-examination, 
5  contrary evidence, and careful instruction on the burden of proof, not exclusion.  Daubert, 
6
509 U.S. at 596
.  The judge is “to screen the jury from unreliable nonsense opinions, but 
7  not exclude opinions merely because they are impeachable.”  Alaska Rent-A-Car, Inc. v. 
8  Avis Budget Grp., Inc.,
738 F.3d 960, 969
 (9th Cir. 2013).  In its role as gatekeeper, the 
9  trial court “is not tasked with deciding whether the expert is right or wrong, just whether 
10  his [or her] testimony has substance such that it would be helpful to a jury.”
Id.
 at 969–70. 
11       The tests for admissibility in general, and reliability in particular, are flexible.  
12  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 564.  The Supreme Court has provided several factors to determine 
13  reliability: (1) whether a theory or technique is testable; (2) whether it has been published 
14  in peer-reviewed literature; (3) the error rate of the theory or technique; and (4) whether it 
15  has been generally accepted in the relevant scientific community.  Elsayed Mukhtar v. Cal. 
16  State Univ., Hayward,
299 F.3d 1053, 1064
 (9th Cir. 2002) (summarizing Daubert, 509 
17  U.S. at 592–94), overruled on other grounds by Est. of Barabin v. AstenJohnson, Inc., 740
18 F.3d 457
, 460 (9th Cir. 2014).  These factors are meant to be “helpful, not definitive.”  
19  Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael,
526 U.S. 137, 151
 (1999).  The court “has discretion to 
20  decide how to test an expert’s reliability as well as whether the testimony is reliable, based 
21  on the particular circumstances of the particular case.”  Primiano, 598 F.3d at 564 (citation 
22  modified).  “[T]he test under Daubert is not the correctness of the expert’s conclusions but 
23  the soundness of his [or her] methodology.”  Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., Inc.,
43 F.3d 24 1311, 1318
 (9th Cir. 1995).  Once the threshold established by Rule 702 is met, the expert 
25  may testify, and the fact finder decides how much weight to give that testimony.  Primiano, 
26  598 F.3d at 565.                                                          
27       After admissibility is established to the court’s satisfaction, attacks aimed at the 
28  weight of the evidence are the province of the fact finder, not the judge.  Pyramid Techs., 
1  Inc. v. Hartford Cas. Ins. Co.,
752 F.3d 807, 814
 (9th Cir. 2014).  The court should not 
2  make credibility determinations that are reserved for the jury.
Id.
      
3  III.  ANALYSIS                                                            
4       Pixels argues Tregillis’s opinions are inadmissible because Tregillis (1) employs a 
5  faulty and unreliable methodology; (2) relies upon insufficient facts and data; and (3) 
6  provides irrelevant factual opinions.  (ECF No. 77 at 2:7-17.)            
7       Pixels does not challenge Tregillis’s qualifications.  (See generally Mot.)  Tregillis 
8  holds an M.B.A. in Finance and Accounting.  (Tregillis Report at App. A.)  He has more 
9  than thirty years of experience analyzing financial, accounting, economic, statistical, and 
10  market issues, primarily relating to disputes, valuations, and license agreements covering 
11  intellectual property rights.  (Id.)  Tregillis has held leadership positions with many public 
12  accounting and licensing professional groups.  (Id.)  He is also accredited in Business 
13  Valuation and certified in Financial Forensics, Public Accounting, and Licensing.  (Id.)  
14  Thus, finding Tregillis sufficiently qualified to render his opinion, the Court turns to Pixels’ 
15  arguments for exclusion.                                                  
16       A.   Methodology                                                     
17       Tregillis  calculates  the  fair  market  value  of  Pixels’  use  of  Jordan’s  rights  by 
18  analyzing comparable licenses for rights similar to those used by Pixels as a starting point 
19  to construct a hypothetical license.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 118-21.)  Tregillis then adjusts the 
20  value of the benchmark comparable license to account for the other athletes included in the 
21  benchmark license, the length of time of Pixels’ use, and the fact that Pixels’ use of Jordan’s 
22  rights was not subject to any quality assurance or approval clauses.  (Id. ¶¶ 122, 126.)  
23  Pixels  argues  that  the  benchmark  agreement  chosen  by  Tregillis  is  insufficiently 
24  comparable and that Tregillis makes improper assumptions to inflate the value of the 
25  benchmark license.  (ECF No. 77 at 9:19–10:1.)                            
26       Damages determined through a hypothetical license are appropriate “provided the 
27  amount is not based on undue speculation.”  See Polar Bear Prods., Inc. v. Timex Corp., 
28
384 F.3d 700
, 709 (9th Cir. 2004) (citation modified); see also Marketquest Grp., Inc. v. 
1  BIC Corp.,
316 F. Supp. 3d 1234, 1300
 (S.D. Cal. 2018) (permitting hypothetical licensing 
2  damages in a Lanham Act dispute “if the evidence provides a sufficiently reliable basis to 
3  calculate such damages”).  “The touchstone for hypothetical-license damages is ‘the range 
4  of [the license’s] reasonable market value.’”  Oracle Corp. v. SAP AG,
765 F.3d 1081
, 
5  1088 (9th Cir. 2014) (quoting Polar Bear Prods., 384 F.3d at 709).  “The question, 
6  therefore, is not what the owner would have charged, but rather what is the fair market 
7  value.”  Id. (citation modified).                                         
8       Accordingly,  as  a  starting  point,  Tregillis’s  methodology  of  constructing  a 
9  hypothetical license to determine the fair market value of Pixels’ use of Jordan’s rights is 
10  an accepted and reliable method to calculate damages in an intellectual property dispute.  
11  See Polar Bear Prods., 384 F.3d at 709.  The Court now considers the reliability of the 
12  facts underlying Tregillis’s methodology and opinions.                    
13            1.   Underlying Facts and Data                                  
14       Tregillis determines the Trends Agreement to be the most comparable to the facts at 
15  issue here and uses this agreement as the benchmark for his hypothetical license analysis.  
16  (Tregillis Report ¶ 121.)  The Trends Agreement was a licensing agreement between 
17  Brevettar,  described  as  “the  exclusive  licensing  agent  for  Upper  Deck,”  and  Trends 
18  International, LLC.  (Id. ¶ 50.)  The Trends Agreement granted Trends a license to 
19  manufacture, distribute, and sell collector’s edition posters and calendars featuring the 
20  name, image, likeness, signature, and statistical data of Michael Jordan, Wayne Gretzky, 
21  and Tiger Woods.  (Id.)  A later amendment to the Trends Agreement also allowed Trends 
22  to sell canvas wall décor.  (Id. ¶¶ 56–57.)                               
23       Pixels argues that the Trends Agreement is an improper comparable because Upper 
24  Deck  was not  a  party to it,  Upper Deck  did not  receive  royalty  payments  from  the 
25  agreement, and the Trends Agreement was not effective until two and a half years after 
26  Pixels alleged unauthorized sales began.  (ECF No. 77 at 10:4–11:1.)  Pixels also asserts 
27  that Tregillis improperly inflated the annual minimum guarantee and sales made under the 
28  Trends Agreement by relying on a later amendment to the Trends Agreement that increased 
1  the annual minimum guarantee and added another category of products covered by the 
2  Trends  Agreement.    (Id.  at  11:2–12:10.)    Finally,  Pixels  claims  Tregillis  improperly 
3  deflated the annual minimum guarantee payment to account for the other athletes included 
4  in the Trends Agreement.  (Id. at 12:11-20.)                              
5       When  constructing  a  hypothetical  license,  “the  licenses  relied  on  by  the 
6  [rightsholder] in proving damages [must be] sufficiently comparable to the hypothetical 
7  license at issue in suit.”  Lucent Techs., Inc. v. Gateway, Inc.,
580 F.3d 1301, 1325
 (Fed. 
8  Cir. 2009); see also Marketquest Grp.,
316 F. Supp. 3d at 1300
 (requiring a “sufficiently 
9  reliable basis to calculate. . . damages” in absence of a prior licensing agreement).  As such, 
10  “alleging a loose or vague comparability between different technologies or licenses does 
11  not suffice.”  LaserDynamics, Inc. v. Quanta Comput., Inc.,
694 F.3d 51, 79
 (Fed. Cir. 
12  2012).  However, any hypothetical license analysis “necessarily involves an element of 
13  approximation and uncertainty.”  Lucent,
580 F.3d at 1325
 (citation modified); see also 
14  Skydive Ariz., Inc. v. Quattrocchi,
673 F.3d 1105, 1113
 (9th Cir. 2012) (“We emphasize 
15  that section 1117 confers a wide scope of discretion upon the district judge in fashioning a 
16  remedy.”  (citation modified)).  “[T]he fact that a license is not perfectly analogous 
17  generally goes to the weight of the evidence, not its admissibility.”  Ericsson, Inc. v. D-
18  Link Sys., Inc.,
773 F.3d 1201, 1227
 (Fed. Cir. 2014); see also Roblox Corp. v. WowWee 
19  Grp. Ltd., No. 22-cv-04476-SI,
2024 WL 4057418
, at *14 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 3, 2024) 
20  (rejecting objections that the benchmark license was not sufficiently comparable as the 
21  objections went to the weight, not admissibility of the expert’s analysis). 
22       Here, the Trends Agreement concerned the same rights at issue in this case, Jordan’s 
23  name, image, likeness, and publicity rights.  (Tregillis Report ¶ 50.)  Further, the Trends 
24  Agreement covered the same types of products as those at issue here—posters, calendars, 
25  and wall décor.  (Id. ¶ 121.)  The Trends Agreement also covered products similarly priced 
26  to those sold by Pixels.  (Id.)  Consequently, the Court finds the Trends Agreement 
27  sufficiently comparable to serve as a reliable basis for the hypothetical license analysis 
28  Tregillis conducts.                                                       
1       Each  of  Pixels’  arguments  about  the  specific  terms  of  the  Trends  Agreement, 
2  including the parties to it, the time period it covered, the products it included, the annual 
3  minimum  guarantee,  and  the  proportion  of  sales  attributed to  each  athlete  under  the 
4  Agreement, bears on the Agreement’s comparability with the conduct at issue here.  As 
5  such, these arguments go to the weight of the evidence, not its admissibility.1  See Ericsson, 
6
773 F.3d at 1227
; Roblox Corp.,
2024 WL 4057418
, at *14.                  
7            2.   The Premium Multiplier                                     
8       After identifying the Trends Agreement as the best benchmark for his hypothetical 
9  license analysis, Tregillis uses a premium multiplier to adjust for the fact that Pixels’ use 
10  of Jordan’s rights was not authorized and not subject to the quality assurance and approval 
11  clauses typically included in Jordan’s licensing agreements.  (Tregillis Report ¶ 122.)  
12  Tregillis calculates this multiplier by comparing two similar situations where Jordan’s 
13  rights were used, one of which was authorized (the “Hanes Transaction”) and one of which 
14  was unauthorized (the “Panini Settlement”).  (Id. ¶¶ 124-25.)  Tregillis compares the values 
15  of those transactions to calculate the percentage premium for unauthorized uses of Jordan’s 
16  rights.  (Id.)  Pixels argues that the application of this premium multiplier is unreliable and 
17  that the Hanes Transaction and Panini Settlement are not reliably comparable to the 
18  conduct at issue here.  (ECF No. 77 at 13:5-12.)                          
19        Hypothetical  license  analysis  requires  experts  to  make  adjustments  to  the 
20  benchmark  agreement  to  best  fit  the  facts  at  issue.    Indeed,  upward  and  downward 
21  adjustments to a benchmark agreement are commonly and reliably used in hypothetical 
22  license analyses.  See, e.g., Oracle Am., Inc. v. Google Inc.,
847 F. Supp. 2d 1178
, 1184 
23  (N.D. Cal. 2012) (finding an upward adjustment based on several factually supported 
24  factors to be proper under Daubert); Juno Therapeutics, Inc. v. Kite Pharma, Inc., No. 
25                                                                            
26                                                                            
        1 Pixels’ arguments are further undermined by the fact that Pixels’ own expert not only identifies 
27  the same hypothetical license methodology as one way to calculate damages, but also identifies the Trends 
   Agreement as an instructive comparable.  (See Expert Report of Lindsey Fisher ¶¶ 29, 92, ECF No. 103-
28                                                                            
1  2:17-cv-07639 SJO-KS,
2019 WL 8685065
, at *4–5 (C.D. Cal. Dec. 3, 2019) (finding the 
2  damages expert’s upward adjustment to the royalty rate sufficiently reliable to present to a 
3  jury).  However, such adjustments must be based on non-speculative evidence to be 
4  sufficiently reliable.  See Oracle Corp.,
765 F.3d at 1088
 (“An award of hypothetical-
5  license damages is appropriate provided the amount is not based on undue speculation.”  
6  (citation modified)).                                                     
7       Here, the adjustment Tregillis applies is neither created out of whole cloth nor based 
8  on mere speculation, as Pixels asserts.  Rather, Tregillis demonstrates the necessity of this 
9  premium  adjustment  by  discussing  Jordan’s  carefully  tailored  brand  and  restrictive 
10  approach to licensing agreements.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 88–106.)  Then, Tregillis conducts 
11  a comparative analysis using otherwise analogous transactions to calculate the value of 
12  unauthorized uses of Jordan’s rights.  (Id. ¶¶ 124-25.)  This analysis is grounded in 
13  evidence, and Tregillis’s application of his analysis logically follows.  (See id.)  Therefore, 
14  the premium multiplier calculation and its application to the hypothetical license are 
15  sufficiently reliable to present to a jury.  See Oracle Corp.,
765 F.3d at 1091
. 
16       The cases cited by Tregillis in support of the premium multiplier—and also relied 
17  on by both Pixels and Upper Deck in their briefings—tend to support the reliability of the 
18  premium multiplier in this case.  For example, the Garrapata court, in the default judgment 
19  context, ultimately recognized that “a $2 million figure appropriately compensates [the 
20  plaintiff] for the premium that would be necessarily required to induce it to agree to such 
21  a deal.”  Garrapata, LLC v. Norok Innovation, Inc., No. CV 21-00356-CJC (PDx), 2022
22 WL 4099470
, at *7 (C.D. Cal. May 13, 2022).  In other words, the court recognized that a 
23  premium may be appropriate to incorporate into the damages award to account for the fact 
24  that the plaintiff would not have authorized the use at issue in that case.  Id (“$2 million is 
25  a reasonable representation of the fair market value of Mr. Eastwood’s services in lending 
26  his influential and known name to a hidden metatag campaign for products he likely would 
27  have been unwilling to endorse in the first place.”).  Although Pixels is correct that the 
28  Garrapata court rejected the extent of the premium proposed by the plaintiff, the court 
1  ultimately endorsed the principle of applying a premium to account for unauthorized use.  
2
Id.
 at *6–7.  Tregillis applies that same principle here.                 
3       Likewise, the Edmondson court did not condemn the use of any premium multipliers, 
4  but it rejected the premium multiplier applied by the expert because it was speculative.  
5  Edmondson v. Caliente Resorts, LLC, No. 8:15-cv-2672-T-23TBM,
2017 WL 10591833
, 
6  at *6 (M.D. Fla. Aug. 31, 2017).  The Edmondson expert’s treble multiplier appeared to be 
7  “a formula entirely of [the expert’s] imagination.”
Id.
  But here, in contrast, Tregillis backs 
8  up his premium multiplier by demonstrating why it is appropriate in this case and by 
9  calculating  the  premium  multiplier  through  an  evidence-based  comparative  analysis.  
10  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 88–106, 124-25.)                                     
11       Pixels further attacks on the premium multiplier are similarly unpersuasive.2  Pixels 
12  argues that Tregillis does not properly verify or discuss the Hanes Transaction and Panini 
13  Settlement before using them in his analysis.  (ECF No. 77 at 14:16-20, 15:14–16:8.)  This 
14  argument is unconvincing, as Tregillis spends paragraphs of his report, supported by 
15  citations to the record, discussing the Hanes Transaction and Panini Settlement as well as 
16  how he uses them in his analysis.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 85–86, 124-25.)   
17       Pixels’  next  argument  that  the  Hanes  Transaction  and  Panini  Settlement  are 
18  insufficiently comparable to Pixels’ conduct here misses the point of how Tregillis uses 
19  these two situations.  (ECF No. 77 at 16:28–17:1.)  Tregillis does not use the Hanes 
20  Transaction  and  Panini  Settlement  as  comparable  to  this  case  for  the  purpose  of 
21  hypothetical license analysis; rather, he uses them in a comparative analysis to determine 
22  the value of Jordan’s rights when their use is not subject to any quality assurance or 
23  approval clauses.  (Tregillis Report ¶¶ 124-25.)                          
24                                                                            

25       2 Pixels argues as a “preliminary matter” that the Hanes agreement and its revenue data were not

26  (ECF No. 77 at 13:13–22.)  Upper Deck asserts that Pixels and its experts had time to consider this

28

2  establish damages.  (ECF No. 77 at 15:3-13.)  This argument is contradicted by Ninth 
3  Circuit case law.  See, e.g., Jarvis v. K2 Inc.,
486 F.3d 526, 534
 (9th Cir. 2007) (upholding 
4  the district court’s damages calculations based in part on a prior settlement agreement); 
5  Carucel Invs., L.P. v. Novatel Wireless, Inc.,
2017 WL 1215838
, at *10–11 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 
6  3, 2017) (recognizing that settlement agreements are relevant in determining reasonable 
7  royalty damages).                                                         
8       Accordingly,  the  Court  finds  Tregillis’s  methodology,  including  the  premium 
9  multiplier, as well as the facts and data underlying that methodology to be reliable and 
10  relevant to the task at hand.  See Daubert,
509 U.S. at 597
.              
11       B.   The “Evidence Indicates” Opinions                               
12       In addition to his opinions on the economic harm to Upper Deck and Jordan and the 
13  revenues earned by Pixels, Tregillis offers two “Evidence Indicates” opinions.  First, 
14  “Evidence indicates that, as Upper Deck values its relationship with Jordan, one of the 
15  world’s most iconic athletes and personalities, Upper Deck protects both its rights and 
16  Jordan’s rights, while also ensuring it only produces and/or approves high-quality products 
17  that feature appropriate and value-enhancing uses of Jordan’s rights of publicity and 
18  trademarks.”  (Tregillis Report § 1.1.)  And second, “Evidence indicates that the use made 
19  by Pixels is unauthorized and would not have been authorized by Jordan and/or Upper 
20  Deck.”  (Id.)  Pixels argues these opinions are irrelevant and should be excluded.  (ECF 
21  No. 77 at 21:8-12.)                                                       
22       Expert testimony is relevant if it is sufficiently tied to the facts of the case such that 
23  it will “assist the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue.”  
24  See Daubert,
509 U.S. at 591
 (citation modified).  The Ninth Circuit has found expert 
25  testimony is relevant if it “logically advances a material aspect of the proposing party’s 
26  case.”  Daubert,
43 F.3d at 1315
; see also Primiano, 598 F.3d at 565 (“Expert opinion 
27  testimony is relevant if the knowledge underlying it has a valid connection to the pertinent 
28  inquiry.”  (citation modified)).                                          
1       Pixels primarily argues that the “Evidence Indicates” opinions are irrelevant because 
2  they assert facts favorable to Upper Deck that are not relevant to assisting the jury, and as 
3  such, they should be excluded under Federal Rules of Evidence 702 and 403.  (ECF No. 
4  77 at 21:8-12.)  However, the Court finds that the two “Evidence Indicates” opinions will 
5  aid the jury in understanding Tregillis’s hypothetical license analysis.  The “Evidence 
6  Indicates” opinions shed light on the fair market value of Jordan’s rights as Pixels used 
7  them and demonstrate the necessity of the premium multiplier.  More specifically, the 
8  opinions will help the jury to understand how Upper Deck and Jordan value Jordan’s rights 
9  and typically license them.  Hence, the Court finds that these opinions are relevant for the 
10  jury’s consideration and fall within the scope of Tregillis’s expert testimony.  See Daubert, 
11
43 F.3d at 1315
; Primiano, 598 F.3d at 565.                               
12       Pixels also seems to raise an objection to the “Evidence Indicates” opinions under 
13  Federal Rule of Evidence 704, arguing the second opinion “is a naked attempt to elevate 
14  Upper Deck’s allegations of unauthorized use by Pixels into a liability opinion against 
15  Pixels.”  (See ECF No. 77 at 23:18-20.)  Upper Deck responds by asserting that “Tregillis 
16  is not testifying about ‘authorization’ in a liability sense (he assumes this as all damages 
17  experts do . . .), but rather that the use Pixels made would not have been contractually 
18  approved or authorized by Jordan because of the images used and types of products sold.  
19  This goes to brand standards, not liability.”  (ECF No. 100 at 22:20-24.) 
20       Under Federal Rule of Evidence 704, “[a]n opinion is not objectionable just because 
21  it embraces an ultimate issue.”  Rather, the basic approach to opinions is to admit them 
22  when helpful to the trier of fact.  Fed. R. Evid. 704 advisory committee’s notes.  Experts 
23  may not, however, offer opinions embodying legal conclusions.  See id. (clarifying Rule 
24  704 as not permitting “the admission of opinions which would merely tell the jury what 
25  result to reach”).                                                        
26       Here, the Court agrees that Tregillis’s second “Evidence Indicates” opinion goes to 
27  brand standards and addresses how the fair market value of Jordan’s rights is impacted 
28  when subject to quality assurance and approval clauses.  This opinion lays the foundation 
|        Tregillis’s use of the premium multiplier to  account for the  fact that Pixels’  use  of

20         Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES Pixels’ motion to exclude the testimony 
21        Upper  Deck’s  expert.   (ECF  No.  77.)   The  Court  finds  Christian  Tregillis  is  duly

23  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
24       Defendant Pixels.com (“Pixels”) allegedly interfered with Upper Deck’s exclusive 
25  rights  to  use  intellectual  property  assets  associated  with  the  brand  of  world-famous
